questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Why did Indian merchants and industrialists support the Civil Disobedience Movement ? Explain.
questions.solution: During the First World War they had made large profits and wanted to expand. They wanted protection against imports of foreign goods and a rupee–sterling exchange ratio that would discourage imports, so they opposed colonial policies that restricted business. They saw swaraj as a time when such restrictions would end, so they gave financial help and refused to buy or sell imported goods.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Examine the significance of pipeline as a means of transportation in the country.
questions.solution: Pipelines carry crude oil, petroleum products, natural gas (and water) from oil and gas fields to refineries, fertiliser factories and power plants, even far inland. The initial cost is high but running costs are minimal; they avoid transhipment losses and delays and can cross difficult terrain. They have helped set up refineries and gas-based industries in places such as Barauni, Mathura and Panipat.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Why has India adopted a multi-party system ? Explain.
questions.solution: India is a large country with great social and geographical diversity: many religions, castes, languages and regions. Such diversity cannot easily be absorbed by two or three parties. A multiparty system allows a variety of interests and opinions to get political representation, and parties can form coalitions to govern.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: How is 'Demand Deposit' an essential feature of money ?
questions.solution: Deposits in bank accounts can be withdrawn on demand, so they are called demand deposits. They can be used for payments through cheques (and digital transfers) instead of cash, so they share the essential features of money: a medium of exchange that is widely accepted. Modern money therefore includes demand deposits as well as currency.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text:
The textile production chain runs: Fibre production → Raw fibre → Spinning → Yarn → Weaving/Knitting → Fabric → Dyeing and finishing → Garment manufacture → Garments.
(5.1) Which is the basic material required for garment manufacturing ?
(5.2) Give one example of value addition in the textile industry.
questions.solution: (5.1) Fabric (made from yarn spun from raw fibre). (5.2) Any one: spinning raw fibre into yarn; weaving yarn into fabric; dyeing and finishing the fabric; stitching it into garments. Each step adds value to the product.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Differentiate between formal and informal sources of Credit.
questions.solution: Formal sources (banks, cooperatives) are supervised by the Reserve Bank of India, charge lower interest, usually need collateral and documents, and aim at social welfare as well. Informal sources (moneylenders, traders, employers, relatives, friends) are not supervised, charge much higher interest and may use unfair means to recover loans, often trapping borrowers in debt.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: How does a bank work as a key component of the financial system ? Explain.
questions.solution: Banks accept deposits from people with surplus money and pay them interest. They keep only a small part (about 15%) as cash for withdrawals and lend the rest to people and businesses that need funds. They charge a higher interest on loans than they pay on deposits, and the difference is their income. So banks mediate between savers and borrowers and keep money circulating in the economy.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: "It was essential to preserve folk tradition in order to discover one's national identity and restore a sense of pride in one's past." Support the statement in reference to India.
questions.solution: In the late 19th century, Indian nationalists began recording folk tales sung by bards and touring villages to gather folk songs and legends, believing they gave a true picture of traditional culture that had been damaged by outside forces. Rabindranath Tagore led the revival of folk culture in Bengal, and Natesa Sastri published a collection of Tamil folk tales, The Folklore of Southern India. This helped Indians discover their identity and take pride in their past.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Explain the role of Election Commission in the 'registration and recognition' of political parties in India.
questions.solution: Every party in India has to register with the Election Commission. The Commission treats all parties as equal but gives special facilities to large, established parties, which are 'recognised' and given a unique symbol that only their official candidates can use. A party that gets at least 6% of the votes in a state assembly election and wins at least two seats is recognised as a state party; one that gets at least 6% of votes in Lok Sabha or assembly elections in four states and wins at least four Lok Sabha seats is recognised as a national party.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: "Democracy is a better form of government than any other alternative." Analyse the statement.
questions.solution: Democracy promotes equality among citizens and enhances the dignity of the individual; it improves the quality of decision-making through discussion and consultation; it provides a method to resolve conflicts peacefully; it allows room to correct mistakes; and it produces an accountable, responsive and legitimate government chosen by the people.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text: Analyse the reasons for the overwhelming support for the idea of democracy all over the world.
questions.solution: Democracy gives an accountable, responsive and legitimate government; it promotes equality, dignity and freedom of citizens, including women and disadvantaged groups; it accommodates social diversity and resolves conflicts peacefully; it allows mistakes to be corrected through elections and public criticism; and people prefer being ruled by representatives they choose. That is why over a hundred countries claim to be democracies and people everywhere support the idea.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.chapter: Economics: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
questions.text: Examine the factors which facilitate globalization in India.
questions.solution: 1. Technology: faster, cheaper transport (containers, aircraft) and information and communication technology (telephones, mobiles, internet) let goods, services and information move quickly. 2. Liberalisation of foreign trade and investment from 1991, which removed barriers on imports and foreign investment. 3. Pressure from international organisations such as the WTO to open up trade. 4. Policies such as SEZs and tax incentives that attracted MNCs. Together these integrated India with world markets.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.chapter: Economics: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
questions.text: Assess, how globalization has touched the lives of larger society.
questions.solution: Well-off urban consumers have more choice, better quality and lower prices. New jobs have been created in MNCs and in companies supplying them, and services such as IT have grown, while some Indian firms have become MNCs. But small producers in industries such as toys, batteries and plastics have faced tough competition and many have closed, and many workers now have insecure, flexible jobs with low wages and few benefits. So the gains have not been shared equally, and fair globalisation needs government action.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text:
The Independence Day Pledge, 26 January, 1930: 'We believe that it is the inalienable right of the Indian people, as of any other people, to have freedom and to enjoy the fruits of their toil and have the necessities of life, so that they may have full opportunities of growth. We believe also that if any government deprives a people of these rights and oppresses them, the people have a further right to alter it or to abolish it. The British Government in India has not only deprived the Indian people of their freedom but has based itself on the exploitation of the masses, and has ruined India economically, politically, culturally, and spiritually. We believe, therefore, that India must sever the British connection and attain Purna Swaraj or Complete Independence.'

Why was freedom considered an inalienable right of the Indian people ?
questions.solution: Because, like any other people, Indians had the right to freedom, to enjoy the fruits of their toil and have the necessities of life so they could grow fully; it cannot be taken away.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text:
The Independence Day Pledge, 26 January, 1930: 'The British Government in India has not only deprived the Indian people of their freedom but has based itself on the exploitation of the masses, and has ruined India economically, politically, culturally, and spiritually.'

Why was Purna Swaraj considered essential by the people of India ?
questions.solution: Because British rule had denied Indians freedom, exploited the masses and ruined India economically, politically, culturally and spiritually, so complete independence was the only remedy.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text:
The Independence Day Pledge, 26 January, 1930: 'We believe, therefore, that India must sever the British connection and attain Purna Swaraj or Complete Independence.'

Explain the significance of the Lahore Session of Congress.
questions.solution: At the Lahore Congress (December 1929), under Jawaharlal Nehru, the demand for Purna Swaraj (complete independence) was formalised. It was declared that 26 January 1930 would be celebrated as Independence Day, with people pledging to struggle for complete independence. It prepared the ground for the Civil Disobedience Movement.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text:
Lifelines of National Economy: For a long time, trade and transport were restricted to a limited space. With the development in science and technology, the area of influence of trade and transport expanded far and wide. Today, the world has been converted into a large village with the help of efficient and fast moving transport. Transport has been able to achieve this with the help of equally developed communication system. Therefore, transport, communication and trade are complementary to each other. Today, India is well-linked with the rest of the world despite its vast size, diversity and linguistic and socio-cultural plurality. Railways, airways, waterways, newspapers, radio, television, cinema and internet, etc. have been contributing to its socio-economic progress in many ways.

How is science an important factor in the development of transport ?
questions.solution: Advances in science and technology produced faster and more efficient means of transport and communication, which expanded the area of trade and transport far and wide.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text:
Lifelines of National Economy: Today, India is well-linked with the rest of the world despite its vast size, diversity and linguistic and socio-cultural plurality.

How has transport integrated socio-cultural plurality ? Explain.
questions.solution: By connecting distant regions, transport lets people of different languages and cultures travel, trade and interact, bringing them closer and promoting national unity.

questions.subject: Social Science
questions.text:
Lifelines of National Economy: Transport has been able to achieve this with the help of equally developed communication system. Therefore, transport, communication and trade are complementary to each other.

Analyse the significance of communication for a nation.
questions.solution: Communication (post, telephones, internet, mass media) spreads information and ideas quickly across the country, supports trade and business, helps the government reach citizens, spreads awareness about national programmes and policies, provides education and entertainment, and helps bind a diverse nation together.
